sql_schemas: table employees | fields: id, first_name, last_name, email, role, manager_id, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | fks: manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: email: unique lookup for authentication and employee search; manager_id: frequent queries to find direct reports of a manager; role: filtering employees by role for RBAC and approval routing

table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type, start_date, end_date, reason, status, manager_id, manager_comment, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: employee_id: frequent lookups of leave requests by employee; manager_id: managers querying pending approvals for their team; status: filtering by status (pending/approved/rejected) is the most common access pattern; leave_type: reporting and balance calculations grouped by leave type; start_date, end_date: date-range queries for calendar views and overlap detection

table leave_balances | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type, entitled_days, used_days, year, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id | indexes: employee_id, leave_type, year: unique composite lookup for balance queries per employee per leave type per year; this is the dominant access pattern; employee_id: balance summary views for a single employee across all leave types; year: annual rollover and archival queries

table leave_policies | fields: id, leave_type, max_days_per_year, max_consecutive_days, requires_attachment, year, created_at, updated_at | pk: id | indexes: leave_type: policy lookup by leave type is the primary access pattern; year: policies can change annually

table audit_logs | fields: id, entity_type, entity_id, action, changed_by, old_values, new_values, created_at | pk: id | fks: changed_by -> employees.id | indexes: entity_type, entity_id: audit trail lookups for a specific entity (e.g., all changes to a leave request); changed_by: audit queries by user who performed the action; action: filtering audit logs by action type (create/update/delete/approve/reject); created_at: time-range audit queries

methods: findOverlapping(employeeId: string, startDate: Date, endDate: Date): Promise<LeaveRequest[]>
updateStatus(id: string, status: string, managerId: string, comment?: string): Promise<LeaveRequest>
findByEmployeeLeaveTypeAndYear(employeeId: string, leaveType: string, year: number): Promise<LeaveBalance | null>
upsertBalance(employeeId: string, leaveType: string, year: number, entitledDays: number, usedDays: number): Promise<LeaveBalance>
incrementUsedDays(employeeId: string, leaveType: string, year: number, days: number): Promise<LeaveBalance>
findByLeaveTypeAndYear(leaveType: string, year: number): Promise<LeavePolicy | null>
upsertPolicy(leaveType: string, year: number, maxDaysPerYear: number, maxConsecutiveDays: number, requiresAttachment: boolean): Promise<LeavePolicy>

data_notes: All five conceptual table specs and five repository interfaces are defined. Tables: employees (self-referencing manager hierarchy), leave_requests (core entity with dual FK to employees for employee and manager), leave_balances (per-employee per-leave-type per-year tracking), leave_policies (configurable rules per leave type per year), and audit_logs (GP-002 compliance for all state-changing operations). Repositories all backed by PostgreSQL via the existing pg Pool at src/shared/db/connection.ts. Index rationale reflects dominant access patterns: employee lookups, status filtering, date-range queries, and composite balance lookups. No DDL produced — the code agent generates migrations from these specs.
